section.title: Paul before Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
section.sectionRationale: A new governor inherits Paul's case, and the old plot revives. Pressed to be handed back to Jerusalem, Paul plays the one card a Roman citizen holds and appeals to Caesar. In a single sentence the destination of the whole book is fixed: to Caesar you will go. Festus then stages a hearing before King Agrippa to make sense of a charge he cannot understand, a dispute about a dead man whom Paul says is alive.
section.thesis: When justice bends to political favor, Paul appeals to Caesar and seals his road to Rome; and a baffled governor confesses that the whole case comes down to one thing, a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirms to be alive.
section.frameNote: Four movements: Festus faces the renewed plot against Paul; Paul appeals to Caesar and his course to Rome is set; Festus lays the puzzling case before King Agrippa; and Paul is brought with pomp before the assembled court.

verses.text: Three days after his arrival in the province, Festus went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem,
where the chief priests and Jewish leaders presented their case against Paul. They urged Festus
to grant them a concession against Paul by summoning him to Jerusalem, because they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way.
But Festus replied, “Paul is being held in Caesarea, and I myself am going there soon.
So if this man has done anything wrong, let some of your leaders come down with me and accuse him there.”
After spending no more than eight or ten days with them, Festus went down to Caesarea. The next day he sat on the judgment seat and ordered that Paul be brought in.
When Paul arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they could not prove.
Then Paul made his defense: “I have committed no offense against the law of the Jews or against the temple or against Caesar.”
But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem to stand trial before me on these charges?”
Paul replied, “I am standing before the {{bema|judgment seat}} of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well.

If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to their accusations against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I {{epikaloumai|appeal}} to Caesar!”
Then Festus conferred with his council and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!”

units.label: Festus lays the case before Agrippa
units.note: a dispute about a dead man said to be alive

verses.text: After several days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice came down to Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
Since they were staying several days, Festus laid out Paul’s case before the king: “There is a certain man whom Felix left in prison.
While I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews presented their case and requested a judgment against him.
I told them that it is not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has had an opportunity to face his accusers and defend himself against their charges.
So when they came here with me, I did not delay. The next day I sat on the judgment seat and ordered that the man be brought in.
But when his accusers rose to speak, they did not charge him with any of the crimes I had expected.
They only had some contentions with him regarding their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died, but whom Paul affirmed to be {{zao|alive}}.
Since I was at a loss as to how to investigate these matters, I asked if he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be tried there on these charges.
But when Paul appealed to be held over for the decision of the {{sebastos|Emperor}}, I ordered that he be held until I could send him to Caesar.”
Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” “Tomorrow you will hear him,” Festus declared.

units.label: The prisoner presented with pomp
units.note: no charge to write against him

verses.text: The next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp and entered the auditorium, along with the commanders and leading men of the city. And Festus ordered that Paul be brought in.

Then Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man. The whole Jewish community has petitioned me about him, both here and in Jerusalem, crying out that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he has now appealed to the Emperor, I decided to send him.

I have nothing definite to write to our sovereign about him. Therefore I have brought him before all of you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry I may have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send on a prisoner without specifying the charges against him.”

bema.gloss: A raised platform or tribunal, the seat from which a magistrate gave judgment. Festus sits on the bema, and Paul says he is already standing before the bema of Caesar. The word carries a deeper echo in the New Testament, where all must appear before the judgment seat, the bema, of God, Romans 14:10.

epikaloumai.gloss: To call upon, to invoke, and in legal use to appeal to a higher court. As a Roman citizen Paul formally appeals to Caesar, taking the case out of provincial hands. The same verb is used for calling on the name of the Lord to be saved; Paul the citizen appeals to Caesar, but his hope rests in a higher throne.

zao.gloss: To live, to be alive. Festus reduces the whole controversy to one baffling point: a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul kept insisting was alive. Without knowing it, the puzzled governor names the very heart of the gospel, the resurrection of the crucified Jesus.

sebastos.gloss: The revered or august one, the Greek rendering of the Latin title Augustus given to the Roman emperor. Paul appeals to the Sebastos, the highest earthly authority; yet the book has already shown that Jesus is Lord over Caesar, and the gospel is bound for Rome to declare it.

basic.context: Two years after Felix left him in prison, Paul faces a new governor, Festus. The Jerusalem leaders immediately press to have Paul sent up to them, planning another ambush. Festus refuses to move the venue that far but offers a compromise. To escape being handed back, Paul exercises his right as a Roman citizen and appeals to Caesar, which settles his journey to Rome. Festus then consults the visiting King Agrippa about how to frame the charges.
basic.hermeneutics: Follow the legal maneuvering. The Jews want the trial moved to Jerusalem; Festus wants to please them without breaking Roman custom; Paul refuses the trap and appeals to Caesar. The climax is the appeal in verses 10 to 12. Then watch how Festus, in explaining the case to Agrippa, unwittingly states the gospel: the dispute is about a dead man Paul says is alive.
basic.originalLanguages: Festus sits on the bema, the judgment seat, and Paul says he already stands before Caesar's bema. Paul makes the formal appeal, epikaloumai, that only a citizen could make. Festus sums up the whole matter as a question about whether Jesus is zao, alive. And Paul appeals to the sebastos, the august emperor, though a greater Lord is really in charge.
basic.typology: Paul, innocent yet handed toward Rome by the appeal, walks a road patterned on his Lord, who was also declared innocent by his judges yet delivered up. The Roman insistence that a prisoner face his accusers, and the repeated verdict of no wrong, echo the innocence of Christ before Pilate.
basic.christ: Festus cannot see it, but the case turns entirely on Jesus. The one point he can identify is a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. That is the resurrection, the pivot of the gospel. Every court in these chapters keeps circling the empty tomb, because the risen Christ is the reason Paul stands there at all.
basic.god: God is steering the story. The plot to kill Paul fails; the appeal to Caesar succeeds; and the promise that Paul would testify in Rome moves toward fulfillment. Human schemes and imperial procedures alike serve the purpose of God to carry His witness to the heart of the empire.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 23:11 promised Paul would testify in Rome. Acts 9:15 called him to carry Christ's name before kings. Romans 14:10 speaks of standing before the judgment seat of God. Philippians 1:12 to 13 shows Paul's chains advancing the gospel even in Rome.
basic.oneStory: The ascended Christ is bringing His gospel to the ends of the earth, and here the road to Rome is locked in. An appeal that looks like a legal tactic is in fact the hand of God, carrying His servant, and His witness to the risen Jesus, straight to Caesar's court.

context.literary:
Acts 25 is the middle panel of a triptych of hearings, and Luke arranges it as a double telling. The first half, verses 1 to 12, shows the trial as it happened: the leaders in Jerusalem press, Festus defers, the hearing in Caesarea fails to prove anything, and Paul's appeal closes the door on Jerusalem. The second half, verses 13 to 27, tells the same story again from the governor's point of view, in a speech to a visiting king. Luke is fond of this kind of retelling, and it lets the reader compare the facts with the way a Roman official spins them.

The comparison is revealing. In verse 18 Festus says the accusers did not charge Paul with any of the crimes he had expected. In verse 19 he reduces the whole dispute to contentions about their own religion and a certain Jesus who had died but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. He leaves out his own motive in verse 9, wishing to do the Jews a favor, and in verse 20 he recasts his proposal to move the trial as a question of procedure, being at a loss. The retelling polishes the governor and tidies the facts, and yet it gets the heart of the matter right: the whole dispute is about a dead man said to be alive.

The chapter is also a study in pomp and plainness. Verse 23 describes Agrippa and Bernice entering with great ceremony and an audience of officers and leading men. Paul, the prisoner in the middle of the room, is the only one with a message worth hearing. The governor's closing admission in verses 26 and 27, that he has nothing definite to write to his sovereign and that it seems unreasonable to send a prisoner without specifying the charges, ends the chapter on an unintended confession of the emptiness of the case.
context.historical:
Porcius Festus succeeded Felix as procurator of Judea around AD 59 or 60 and died in office a couple of years later. Josephus gives him a better name than Felix: he moved against the bandits who plagued the countryside and tried to restore order. His difficulty, as Luke shows, was that he inherited a difficult province and a prisoner whose case had been left unresolved. His first act is to go up to Jerusalem, where the chief priests press him for a favor. Luke's note that they were preparing an ambush on the road in verse 3 shows that the plot of Acts 23 had not died during Paul's two years in prison.

Festus's reply in verse 16, that it is not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he has faced his accusers, reflects a principle of Roman procedure that Luke clearly admires. The appeal to Caesar was a right of a Roman citizen. In the early empire the appeal protected a citizen from the harsh discretion of a provincial magistrate, and by Paul's day it could carry a case to the emperor himself. Festus first consults his council, the group of advisers a governor kept, and then accepts the appeal, as verse 12 records. Once Paul has appealed, neither he nor the governor can easily withdraw it, as Agrippa notes in Acts 26:32.

Marcus Julius Agrippa, known as Agrippa II, was the son of the Herod Agrippa who executed James and then died in Acts 12:21 to 23. He ruled territories in the north and east, and had been given a say over the temple and the appointment of its high priests, which is why Festus thinks he can help. His sister Bernice came with him. The emperor at this time was Nero, though Festus calls him only 'our sovereign' in verse 26.

Caesarea was the seat of Roman rule, a port city on the coast built by Herod the Great, with a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles. The great hall in verse 23 was large enough for officers and the leading men of the city to attend, and the whole scene is meant to be impressive. The commanders of the garrison are there for the show.
context.canonical:
The chapter belongs to a thread of promises about Paul and about kings. At his call the Lord said that Paul would carry His name before Gentiles and their kings, Acts 9:15, and in Luke 21:12 to 13 Jesus told all His followers that when they were brought before kings and governors it would become an opportunity to witness. Acts 25 is the point where the second of those words becomes literal: a king, a governor and an audience of officers will hear the gospel, whether or not they intend to.

The appeal to Caesar fulfills the Lord's word in Acts 23:11, you must testify in Rome. The Lord's promise rests on a human process, a prisoner's legal right. Paul will later look back on this road in Philippians 1:12 to 14, where he writes that his circumstances have served to advance the gospel, with the whole palace guard learning that he is in chains for Christ. The route that began with a plot in Jerusalem ends in the emperor's household.

Festus's summary of the case in verse 19 is a quiet echo of the whole New Testament message. A certain Jesus, who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive. It echoes the resurrection testimony of 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 8 and the proclamation in Acts 2:24 that God raised Him up. Even an unbelieving governor cannot help stating the creed.

The chapter also recalls Jesus' own trials. Pilate declared Jesus innocent and still handed Him over, Luke 23:14 to 15, and in John 19:12 the leaders pressed with the threat that anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar. In Acts 25 it is Paul who appeals to Caesar rather than being handed over. The Lord's servant uses the system that once condemned his Lord, a sign that the powers of the world are being used, against their will, to carry His message. Paul will write in Romans 13:1 to 7 about the place of such authorities under God.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wants his readers, many of whom would be Gentile and some perhaps Roman, to see that the Roman authorities found Paul innocent time after time. Festus says it in verse 25, I found he had done nothing worthy of death, and Agrippa says it in 26:32. The Christian message is not a threat to the order of the empire, and Luke has taken care to record that officials on the spot knew it.

He also wants to expose how weak the accusation was. The charges in verse 7 were many and serious, and they could not be proved. The governor cannot name a single crime. This is not only a matter of law. It is Luke's way of showing that the real quarrel is a religious one, about a Jesus who is alive, and that the world's courts have no category for it.

Third, he wants his readers to see how God uses what looks like Paul's misfortune. A second hearing, a governor's wish to please, a compromise offered in Jerusalem, all push toward the appeal. By the end of the chapter, Paul has what the Lord promised, a way to Rome, though by a route no one planned. Luke invites readers to trust the same God for their own unplanned roads.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter reports what Paul did, and it does not tell believers to appeal to the government whenever they are in trouble. Paul used a right he had as a Roman citizen, much as he had used it in Philippi in Acts 16:37 and in Jerusalem in Acts 22:25. His appeal is a prudent act, not a rule.

What the passage invites is a thoughtful use of legitimate means. Paul declares that he is willing to die if he is guilty, verse 11, and yet he refuses to be handed over to people who plan to kill him without a fair hearing. He sets his integrity and his safety side by side. The principle is that faithful people may use lawful protections without thinking that using them shows a lack of faith.

It would be a mistake to take verse 11 as a general statement that Christians should avoid martyrdom. Elsewhere Paul says he is ready to face death and counts his life of no value if only he may finish his course, Acts 20:24. The point here is narrower: Paul will not hand himself to a murder plot, but he does not refuse to die if the cause is just. Festus's description of his own unwillingness to hand a man over without a hearing is also a description, and believers can take from it the idea that a fair process matters, without treating the governor as a model of virtue.

debates.question: Was Paul right to appeal to Caesar rather than trust God more directly?

views.label: Yes, it was wise and in line with God's plan
views.case: The appeal used a legal right to avoid a handover that would have meant ambush and death, and it fit the Lord's promise in Acts 23:11. Luke gives no hint of criticism, and the Lord had already told Paul he would reach Rome.

views.label: It was a mistake that kept Paul in prison longer
views.case: Agrippa says in Acts 26:32 that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed. Some readers think Paul missed a chance to go free, and that his need to appeal came from trusting legal means rather than waiting for God to open the prison door.

views.label: Both: a human choice inside a divine promise
views.case: Luke shows God's promise and Paul's decision together. Paul could not know how things would turn out; he chose a safe course in a dangerous case, and God used it. This is how Acts often works: the Lord's will and human decisions are woven together without one cancelling the other.

debates.bearing: Luke does not pass judgment on the choice. He lets the outcome show that God was at work, and Agrippa's comment makes plain that the road to Rome had a price. The passage teaches that a faithful use of ordinary means is not the opposite of trusting God, and that the cost of a path may be higher than we expect.

debates.question: Why does Luke give so much space to Roman trials of Paul?

views.label: To show that Christianity is no threat to Rome
views.case: Repeated verdicts of innocence, from Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa, suggest an apology for the faith: Christians are not revolutionaries. Some scholars see Luke writing partly to help Roman readers or officials see this.

views.label: To show how the gospel advances to the center of power
views.case: The trials move step by step up the ladder of authority toward Caesar. The point, on this view, is not so much to defend the church as to show that the word of the Lord reaches kings, as Acts 9:15 had said.

views.label: To show Paul as a faithful witness who follows his Lord
views.case: The trials echo the trials of Jesus, and so the chapter shows a disciple sharing his master's path. Luke wants readers to see Paul's patience and clarity as a pattern for believers who face hostile courts.

debates.bearing: These purposes are compatible, and Luke likely held all of them. Whichever is emphasized, the chapter makes the same central point: the case turns on Jesus' resurrection, and the Roman world can neither prove a crime nor ignore the claim.

study.originalLanguages:
The Greek of the chapter makes several points that translations flatten. In verses 3 and 9 the word is charis, a favor. The leaders ask Festus to do them a favor against Paul, and Festus, wishing charin katathesthai, to lay up a favor with the Jews, offers to move the trial. In Paul's reply in verse 11 the word he uses for hand me over is charisasthai, from the same family, to give up as a favor. Paul quietly points out what is going on: a man's life is being treated as a gift between politicians. His answer, that no one has the right to give him away, uses the word that exposes the whole business.

The accusation in verse 3 was an ambush, enedra, a lying in wait; the same word occurs in Acts 23:16 for the plot of the forty. The letter and the hearing are both reminders that the old plan never went away. The charges that could not be proved, aitiomata in verse 7, are accusations or grounds of blame, and the word suggests a case that has volume but no weight.

Festus describes the dispute in verse 19 as a matter of deisidaimonia. The word is a double one: in a favorable sense it means reverence for the divine, and in an unfavorable sense it means superstition. In Acts 17:22 Paul uses the related comparative of the Athenians, deisidaimonesterous, 'very religious'. The word used here by a Roman shows a man who regards the whole controversy as a matter of an alien cult, something outside his competence. The phrase is a polite way of dismissing a question that is about the truth of the universe.

When Festus says he does not know how to proceed, in verse 20, he uses aporeo, to be at a loss. The same family of words appears in Luke 24:4 and Acts 25:20 for people who find no way through. It is an accurate description of the world before Jesus: it has no category for a man who is dead and alive.

In verse 26 Festus says he has nothing definite to write to 'our sovereign', and the Greek is to kyrio, the lord. It is the word the church uses for Jesus, and in this chapter the empire's lord and the church's Lord stand in the same room. Festus describes Nero as the one to whom he must write. The reader knows that a Lord who stood by Paul in Acts 23:11 has already written the next chapter.

Finally, verse 23 says Agrippa and Bernice enter meta pollas phantasias, with great pomp or display. The word phantasia gives us fantasy, and here it means show, an outward display with little behind it. Luke is hinting that the real authority in the room is not the one making the most noise.

typology.type: The innocent one handed over to be judged, Luke 23:14 to 25
typology.fulfillment: Pilate declared Jesus not guilty and still handed Him over, Luke 23:14 to 15; Festus finds nothing worthy of death in Paul, verse 25, and still sends him on. In both cases the verdict of innocence has no power to free. The escalation is that Jesus' handing over was the means of salvation, Acts 2:23, while Paul's is a means of mission. The type falls short in that Paul's innocence is relative, as he admits elsewhere, while Christ's is perfect, 1 Peter 2:22.

typology.type: The bema, the seat of judgment
typology.fulfillment: Festus sits on the bema, and Paul says he stands at Caesar's bema, verse 10. The scene is a picture of a greater one: all believers must appear before the judgment seat of Christ, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10. The correspondence is that human courts, however flawed, foreshadow a final court. The escalation is that this judge sees what governors cannot, Hebrews 4:13. The type falls short because Roman justice is partial and political, while the judgment of Christ is perfect, and for His people it falls on Him first.

typology.type: A dead man said to be alive, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: Festus's summary is unintended gospel. The resurrection of Jesus is the center of apostolic preaching, Acts 17:31 and 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 8. In Old Testament terms, the vindicated sufferer of Psalm 16:10 does not see decay, and Peter applies it to Jesus in Acts 2:27 to 31. The escalation is from a hope to an event: the thing Israel awaited has happened to one man. The pattern falls short in this chapter only because Festus does not grasp what he says.

typology.type: The prisoner who carries the message to the center of power
typology.fulfillment: Paul's road to Rome echoes Joseph's road to Egypt, where a man sold and imprisoned carries God's purposes to the heart of an empire, Genesis 45:5 to 8. It also echoes Daniel before kings, Daniel 6. The escalation is that Paul bears a word of salvation for all nations, not only the survival of a family. The type falls short because Joseph and Daniel were rulers in the end, while Paul remains in chains, Ephesians 6:20, and the glory is Christ's alone.

study.christ:
Christ is the unspoken subject of the chapter. Festus does not know what he is saying when he describes the quarrel as about a certain Jesus who had died but whom Paul affirmed to be alive. He is describing, in the flattest possible way, the center of Christianity. Everything the Jewish leaders brought against Paul comes down to this one disputed fact, and the Roman governor is the first to state it as plainly as a creed.

It matters that this fact is stated of a man named Jesus. The faith of the church is not an idea of immortality or a vague hope for the afterlife. It is the claim that someone who was publicly executed has been raised and is alive. That is why Paul can say in 1 Corinthians 15:14 that if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is useless. The same claim explains why Paul is willing to go to Rome. If Jesus is alive, then He is Lord, and the appeal to the emperor is an appeal in which the true Lord is steering.

There is also a quiet contrast of lords. Festus refers to Nero as 'our sovereign' using the word kyrios. Paul belongs to a Lord whose name is above every name, Philippians 2:9 to 11. Luke has set the two in the same story so that the reader feels the weight of the contrast. The governor cannot say what to write to his lord, because nothing definite can be said against Paul. The church knows what to say of its Lord, because He has done something definite: He has risen.

Christ's own trial hovers over the chapter. Like Jesus, Paul is brought before people who want to do his accusers a favor. Like Jesus, he is declared innocent and still kept in custody. Unlike Jesus, he is not condemned to die, which shows that his sufferings are not a sacrifice for sin. They belong to the Lord's promise that His servants would be brought before kings and governors as witnesses, Luke 21:12 to 13. The One who stood before Pilate has sent a man to stand before Caesar, and what was done once in weakness is now repeated in proclamation. In this sense, the road to Rome is the risen Christ walking His message to the city that thought it ruled the world.
study.god:
God works in this chapter without being named, and the effect is to make His hand easier to see. Think of how many separate decisions lead to Paul's journey to Rome: a leader's plot, a governor's wish to be popular, a compromise offered in Jerusalem, a prisoner's unexpected appeal, a council's quick agreement, a king's curiosity. None of the people involved is acting for the sake of the gospel, and yet every action pushes the same way. Proverbs 21:1 says the king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD, and Luke gives us a courtroom full of examples.

God here is faithful to a specific promise. The Lord had said to Paul, you must testify in Rome, Acts 23:11. Everything in the chapter is the working out of that sentence. The God of Scripture is not only a general sovereign over events; He is a God who speaks particular words and then keeps them. That is why believers can read their own uncertain circumstances with confidence: the same promise-keeping God who ordered the road to Rome is described in Romans 8:28 as working all things together for good for those who love Him.

God's wisdom is also shown in the means. He does not rescue Paul by an angel opening a door, as in Acts 12. He uses a legal right, a citizenship that Paul had inherited, and the slow processes of a Roman court. The same God who can break chains works through paperwork. Scripture holds both together, and a doctrine of God that only allowed miracles would be too small.

The chapter also reveals God as the one before whom every earthly judge will stand. Paul appears at Caesar's bema, but he knows of another bema, Romans 14:10. Festus holds the title of judge, yet the reader sees that the one on trial is not Paul but the world's idea of power. For worship, this means that praise to God includes confidence that no court, council or throne is outside His rule, and that His people may stand before such powers without fear, as Paul does, because the Judge of all the earth will do right, Genesis 18:25.

crossReferences.note: The night word in the barracks named a destination. Paul's cry 'I appeal to Caesar!' in 25:11 is the legal step that puts a ship under him, though no one planned it as a mission. Read together, the two texts show divine word and human decision meeting.

At his call, Paul was named as the Lord's chosen instrument to carry His name before the Gentiles and their kings, and he would suffer for it. Before Festus and Agrippa, with a king in the audience, this word is coming true in a setting no one could have arranged.

Agrippa remarks that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. It is the sequel to this chapter, and it shows the cost of the appeal: the legal door that led to Rome also locked Paul in custody. Luke lets the reader hold both the loss and the purpose.

In Philippi, Paul insisted that officials who had beaten him and Silas without a trial come and escort them out, because they were Roman citizens. His use of citizenship in Acts 25 follows the same pattern of making lawful claims without bitterness, and with the aim of protecting the gospel's reputation.

Paul tells the Romans that all will stand before the judgment seat of God. Set beside Acts 25, where Paul stands at the seat of Festus and speaks of the seat of Caesar, it shows his sense of a higher court that makes all earthly ones relative.

Pilate tells the leaders he has examined Jesus and found Him not guilty, and that neither has Herod. The verdict of innocence is repeated again and again in the passion narrative and again in the story of Paul. In both cases the verdict is real and yet fails to bring release.

Jesus told His disciples that they would be brought before kings and governors on account of His name, and that this would be an opportunity to witness. Acts 25 and 26 show this word at work in the life of Paul, as the court becomes a platform.

Paul's summary of the gospel sets the death, burial and resurrection of Christ as of first importance, with named witnesses. Festus's phrase, a certain Jesus who had died but whom Paul affirmed to be alive, is the same message as seen by an outsider who does not understand it.

Writing from custody, Paul says his circumstances have served to advance the gospel and that the whole palace guard knows he is in chains for Christ. This is the fruit of the road begun here, and shows why the appeal that cost him his freedom did not cost the gospel its progress.

The king's heart is a waterway in the hand of the LORD, who directs it where He pleases. The decisions of Festus, Agrippa and the council in Acts 25 seem to follow their own interests, yet all of them move toward the end God had promised, which is a living example of this proverb.

study.oneStory:
From Genesis onward the Bible asks how the nations, who have turned from God, will hear His word. God's answer in Genesis 12:3 is that all peoples on earth will be blessed through Abraham's offspring. Isaiah says the Servant of the Lord will be a light to the nations, Isaiah 49:6, and the risen Jesus tells His church to be His witnesses to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8. Acts 25 is one of the places where that long answer takes the form of a legal appeal and a boat ticket.

The chapter brings the story to a turning point. Up to now, Paul's travels have been voluntary missionary journeys. From now on he travels as a prisoner under Roman guard, and yet the direction does not change. This is a reversal that the Bible has told before: Joseph is sold and carried to Egypt, and years later says to his brothers that God sent him ahead of them to preserve life, Genesis 45:5 to 8. What others meant for evil, God uses for good, Genesis 50:20. The road to Rome is a new version of that story.

The chapter also shows the empire in its true light. Rome is the greatest power Paul knows, with a procedure for everything, and it cannot find a charge against him. Its officials know the shape of the law, but they cannot see the shape of the gospel. In this way the empire stands in the line of the earlier powers, Egypt, Babylon and Persia, who are used by God without knowing it. Psalm 2 describes the kings of the earth taking their stand against the LORD, and Acts 25 shows a milder, more bureaucratic form of the same thing, along with the surprising result that these same kings are brought within hearing of the Anointed One.

The end of the story lies beyond the chapter. Paul reaches Rome in Acts 28 and proclaims the kingdom of God without hindrance. Beyond that, Revelation 21:24 shows the kings of the earth bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem. The governors and kings of Acts 25, who heard but did not yet believe, stand for the world that will one day bow, and the prisoner whose case they could not name is the first fruit of a gospel that will reach every nation.

quiz.q: Why did Paul appeal to Caesar?

options.text: To avoid being handed back to Jerusalem, where he would face an unjust trial and a plot.
options.note: Festus proposed moving the trial to Jerusalem; Paul, a Roman citizen, appealed to Caesar to escape that trap, verses 9 to 11.

options.text: Because he had a right as a Roman citizen and stood before Caesar's judgment seat.
options.note: True, this is the legal ground of the appeal, but the immediate reason was to escape being sent to Jerusalem.

options.text: Because he wanted to see the city of Rome as a tourist.
options.note: Paul did long to reach Rome for the gospel, but the appeal was a legal move to avoid injustice, not sightseeing.

options.text: Because he admitted he was guilty and sought the emperor's mercy.
options.note: Paul insisted he was innocent; he did not confess guilt.

quiz.q: How does Festus sum up the real dispute when he explains it to Agrippa?

options.text: It concerns a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
options.note: Festus reduces the whole case to the resurrection question, verse 19, the heart of the gospel.

options.text: It is a disagreement about the Jewish religion.
options.note: Festus does call it a matter of their own religion, but he pinpoints it further to the claim that Jesus is alive.

options.text: It is a clear case of sedition against Rome.
options.note: Festus says the opposite; the accusers did not charge Paul with the crimes he had expected.

options.text: It is a property dispute between Paul and the priests.
options.note: Nothing of the kind; the dispute is religious and centers on Jesus and the resurrection.

quiz.q: What did the Jerusalem leaders really want when they asked Festus to summon Paul?

options.text: To ambush and kill him on the road to Jerusalem.
options.note: Luke tells us plainly they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the way, verse 3.

options.text: To have the case tried in Jerusalem rather than Caesarea.
options.note: That was their stated request, but the hidden aim was murder by ambush.

options.text: To give Paul a fairer hearing among his own people.
options.note: The opposite of fairness; they sought his death, not justice.

options.text: To release him quietly to avoid trouble.
options.note: They wanted him dead, not released.

quiz.q: What was Festus's problem as he prepared to send Paul to Rome?

options.text: He had no clear charge to write against a prisoner he found innocent.
options.note: Festus admits he found nothing worthy of death and had nothing definite to write, verses 25 to 27.

options.text: He needed Agrippa's help to understand the Jewish dispute.
options.note: True, he consulted Agrippa, but the root problem was having no real charge to state.

options.text: He was unsure whether Paul was a Roman citizen.
options.note: Citizenship was not the issue; the appeal to Caesar had already been accepted.

options.text: He believed Paul was clearly guilty of a capital crime.
options.note: He believed the opposite; he found Paul had done nothing worthy of death.

quiz.q: How does this chapter show God's purpose at work?

options.text: The plot fails and the appeal sends Paul to Rome, just as the Lord had promised.
options.note: God had said Paul must testify in Rome, Acts 23:11; the events here carry that promise forward.

options.text: God protects Paul from the ambush by keeping him in Caesarea.
options.note: True in part, but the larger point is that the appeal advances God's plan to reach Rome, not merely safety.

options.text: God rewards Paul with immediate release for his patience.
options.note: Paul was not released; he remained a prisoner, yet God's purpose still advanced.

options.text: God's plan is frustrated by the schemes of the powerful.
options.note: The schemes fail; God's purpose to bring Paul to Rome moves steadily forward.

questions: Paul faced renewed danger with steady composure, resting in God's promise that he would reach Rome. Where do you need to trust that God's purpose for you will hold, even under pressure?
Paul used his lawful rights wisely without ever surrendering his trust in God. How do you hold together practical action and faith when facing an unfair situation?
Festus could name Jesus only as a dead man Paul claimed was alive. Who around you knows the name of Jesus but has never faced the question of the resurrection?
God turned a hostile plot and a legal appeal into the road to Rome. Can you look back and see God weaving even opposition into His good purpose for you?
Paul stood before kings and governors as a prisoner, yet kept testifying to Christ. Where has God placed you, however lowly it feels, to bear witness to Him?

translationNotes.note: I appeal to Caesar translates the Greek epikaloumai, a formal legal appeal by which a Roman citizen removed his case to the emperor's court. The same verb elsewhere means to call upon the Lord; the citizen appeals to Caesar, but Scripture points beyond Caesar to a higher throne.

The Emperor and, in verse 26, our sovereign render the Greek Sebastos, the august one, the title Augustus borne by the Roman emperor. Acts uses such titles knowingly, since it everywhere proclaims that Jesus, not Caesar, is Lord of all.

Religion translates a Greek word that can mean religion or superstition; Festus speaks as a puzzled outsider. What he cannot grasp, that a crucified Jesus is alive, is the very center of the Christian message.
